title: Messages, channels and the exchange
summary: What actually travels through an integration, and which slot each piece of data belongs in.

steps.title: Messages and channels
body: The book *Enterprise Integration Patterns* (Hohpe and Woolf, 2003) gave integration a shared vocabulary that
Apache Camel, Spring Integration, MuleSoft and Azure Logic Apps all still use.
- A **message** is what moves: **headers** (key/value metadata) plus a **body** (the payload: JSON, XML, a file, bytes).
- A **channel** is the pipe a message travels on: an HTTP call, a queue, a topic, an in-process hand-off.
- An **endpoint** is where a system connects to a channel.
- A **route** (or pipeline) is a sequence of steps that receives a message from one endpoint and does things to it.
Every bug you will chase in an integration is about **what is in the body or the headers at a given step**.

steps.prompt: Match each kind of message to an example.
pairs: `ReserveStock` for order A1: please do this
The full catalogue record of one book
What is the price of ISBN 9780131103627?
steps.explain: Commands have one intended receiver and can be refused. Events are facts with any number of interested listeners. The difference decides whether you use a queue or a topic later in this module.

steps.title: The exchange
body: Camel wraps each message in an **exchange**: the envelope a route works on. It is the integration's version of
ASP.NET Core's `HttpContext`.
| Slot | Holds | ASP.NET analogy |
| **Body** | the payload | the request/response body |
| **Headers** | metadata that travels *with* the message, and that outgoing components may **send on** | HTTP headers and route values |
| **Properties** | framework-internal values, e.g. the exception the error handler caught | `HttpContext.Items` |
| **Variables** | your own named values that **never leave** the route | local variables in a method |
| **Exception** | set when a step failed | the exception in an exception filter |
It also has an **id** (`exchangeId`), unique per exchange, which makes a perfect trace id.

steps.prompt: Which slot should it live in?
items: The JSON order the customer submitted
The ISBN copied from the path, to build a backend URL three steps later
A running total you compute and use inside the route only
The exception caught by the error handler
The transformed answer you return to the caller
steps.explain: Rule of thumb: if a value must not be sent anywhere, it is a variable. Headers are for things you mean to transmit.

steps.prompt: Why should a header map be a `Dictionary` built with `StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase`?
options: HTTP header names are case-insensitive, so `content-type` and `Content-Type` are the same header
Camel requires all headers to be uppercase
steps.explain: A case-sensitive map would happily hold both `Authorization` and `authorization`, and your "remove Authorization" step would miss one of them.
The second assignment overwrote the first, and `Remove` found `AUTHORIZATION` regardless of case.

steps.title: Copies matter
body: Many patterns (wire tap, splitter, multicast) **copy** an exchange and send the copy somewhere else.
If the copy shares the same header dictionary as the original, a step that changes the copy also changes the
original: a classic source of "a header appeared from nowhere" bugs.
```csharp
var copy = new Exchange { Id = "ex-2", Body = original.Body };
foreach (var (k, v) in original.Headers) copy.Headers[k] = v;   // a real copy
Strings are immutable in .NET, so copying the dictionary entries is enough for a shallow copy.

steps.title: Build an exchange
prompt: - `Dictionary<string, string> Headers`, **case-insensitive**, created by the class (get-only)
- `Dictionary<string, object?> Variables`, created by the class (get-only)
- `Exchange Copy(string newId)`: a new exchange with `newId`, the same body, and **its own** copies of the headers and variables (still case-insensitive headers).
- `string? Header(string name)`: the header's value, or `null` if it is missing.
solution: public Dictionary<string, string> Headers { get; } = new(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
public Dictionary<string, object?> Variables { get; } = new();
var copy = new Exchange { Id = newId, Body = Body };
foreach (var (k, v) in Headers) copy.Headers[k] = v;
foreach (var (k, v) in Variables) copy.Variables[k] = v;
public string? Header(string name) => Headers.TryGetValue(name, out var v) ? v : null;
hints: Initialise the dictionaries in their declarations: `{ get; } = new(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);`
In `Copy`, create `new Exchange { Id = newId, Body = Body }` and loop over both dictionaries.
template: var dojoA = new Exchange { Id = "ex-1", Body = "{\"isbn\":\"1\"}" };
Dojo.Eq("missing header is null", null, dojoA.Header("X-Nope"));
Dojo.Eq("copy has the new id", "ex-2", dojoB.Id);
Dojo.Eq("copy has the same body", dojoA.Body, dojoB.Body);
Dojo.Check("changing the copy's headers leaves the original alone", dojoA.Header("X-Audit") == null, "the copy shares the original's header dictionary");
Dojo.Eq("changing the copy's variables leaves the original alone", (object?)"1", dojoA.Variables["isbn"]);
Dojo.Check("the copy's headers are still case-insensitive", dojoB.Header("x-audit") == "yes", "build the copy's dictionary with StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase");
